Geneva from 20 to 23 October 2026;(b)Approves the provisional agenda of the thirty-third session of the Committee, as set out below:Provisional agenda of the thirty-third session of the Committee of agenda of the thirty-fourth session.7.Arrangements for adopting the report of the Committee on its thirty-third session.Chapter IIIntroduction2.Pursuant to Economic and Social Council resolutions 2004/69 and 2017/2, the thirty-second session of the Committee of Experts on International Cooperation in Tax Matters was held in New York from 23 to 26 March 2026. The session was attended by 23 members of the Committee in person and 2 members virtually, and by 196 registered in-person observers and 137 registered virtual observers.3.The present report serves to summarize Committee discussions and decisions taken on the items set out in the provisional agenda, as adopted by the Committee (E/C.18/2026/1):Provisional agenda1.Opening of the session by the Co-Chairs.2.Adoption of the agenda and organization of work.3.Discussion of issues related to international cooperation in tax matters:(a)Issues related to the United Nations Model Tax Convention;(b)Update of the United Nations Manual for the Negotiation of Bilateral Tax Treaties between Developed and Developing Countries;(c)Transfer pricing;(d)Taxation issues related to the digitalized and globalized economy;(e)Tax administration and artificial intelligence;(f)Taxation of the extractive industries;(g)Indirect taxes;(h)Dispute avoidance and resolution;(i)Environmental taxation;(j)Wealth taxation;(k)Tax and gender;(l)Capacity-building;(m)Other matters for consideration.4.Provisional agenda of the thirty-third session.5.Arrangements for adopting the report of the Committee on its thirty-second session.Chapter IIIOrganization of the sessionOpening of the thirty-second session and adoption of the agenda4.The Co-Chair, Mathew Gbonjubola, spoke at the first open meeting of the session, welcoming members and observers. In his remarks, Mr. Gbonjubola expressed sincere appreciation to the observers for their continued support and to the Secretariat for their dedicated efforts in preparing the session. He further informed participants that, in a closed meeting, the Committee had approved the inclusion of an additional Co-Coordinator for the Subcommittee on Environmental Taxation and confirmed the Co-Coordinators for the Subcommittees on Transfer Pricing and on Taxation Issues related to the Digitalized and Globalized Economy.5.The Director of the Financing for Sustainable Development Office, Shari Spiegel, representing the Secretary-General, noted that during the session the Committee would set priorities and review workplans with a view to forging ahead with its work. She highlighted the importance of mobilizing resources for financing sustainable development due to growing public expenditure needs, geopolitical tensions and declining official development assistance. Promoting inclusive and fair policies was critical amid widening gaps in tax-to-gross domestic product ratios, she added. She noted the Committee’s contributions across key areas, including the United Nations Model Tax Convention and the taxation of high-net-worth individuals, while it encouraged practical and country-driven tax solutions. She extended her wishes for a productive session.6.The Co-Chair introduced the provisional agenda of the thirty-second session (E/C.18/2026/1) and invited the Committee to consider its adoption. The agenda was adopted without amendment.Chapter IVDiscussion and conclusions on substantive issues related to international cooperation in tax mattersA.Issues related to the United Nations Model Tax Convention7.The Co-Coordinators of the Subcommittee on the Update of the United Nations Model Tax Convention, Wanjiru Kiarie and Antoine Guici, introduced conference room paper E/C.18/2026/CRP.1 containing the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan. In line with the priorities endorsed by the Committee at its thirty-first session, the Subcommittee proposed to organize its work around six workstreams: (a) consequential changes related to the subject-to-tax rule, including implications for treaty text and commentary, and interactions with other provisions; (b) treaty definitions with broad cross-cutting relevance and those identified as creating uncertainty or inconsistent application in practice; (c) source rules, including clarification of concepts such as “paid by”, “arising in” and “deemed to arise”, particularly in relation to passive income and cross-border services; (d) attribution of profits to permanent establishments, including issues under article 7 and related commentary; (e) the permanent establishment concept and nexus rules, including consideration of nonphysical presence and emerging business models; and (f) other issues.8.The Co-Coordinators explained that the Subcommittee had organized its proposed workplan around a two-phase approach, with priority initially to be given to workstreams 1 to 3. Workstreams 4 to 6 were proposed for consideration at a later stage, subject to the outcome of ongoing analytical work and any further decisions taken by the Committee at its thirty-third session. They further emphasized that the workstreams were intended to facilitate efficient drafting, coordination and reporting and that the Subcommittee would identify linkages with, and liaise as appropriate with, other relevant subcommittees so as to ensure coherence across the Committee’s outputs.9.During the discussion of the workplan, several members commented on the proposed sequencing, particularly of workstreams 4 and 5. Some members and observers expressed concern that postponing these topics, which they considered highly relevant for developing countries, could leave insufficient time to develop concrete proposals and recommended prioritizing them or launching them in parallel with the initial phase. Views also differed on the relative priority of workstreams 4 and 5. While some members supported the two-phase approach as practical and helpful to avoid duplication, they stressed the need for strong risk mitigation measures. It was further suggested that the Subcommittee could begin work on aspects of the permanent establishment concept that fell outside the scope of the Subcommittee on Taxation of the Digitalized and Globalized Economy.10.Members also emphasized the need for practical coordination with other subcommittees. Although the Subcommittee on Taxation of the Digitalized and Globalized Economy had a narrower focus on services permanent establishments, workstreams 4 and 5 would need to remain closely aligned with both that Subcommittee and the Subcommittee on Transfer Pricing. Suggested approaches to achieving that alignment included overlapping membership, early involvement of those working on workstreams 4 and 5 in related discussions and holding joint meetings where useful. It was also noted that workstream 6 could consider issues arising in other subcommittees, including potential issues under article 22 of the United Nations Model Tax Convention, in coordination with the Subcommittee on Wealth Taxation.11.Members also highlighted several substantive issues across the proposed workstreams. One member underscored the importance of workstream 3, particularly clarifying the terms “paid by”, “arising in” and “deemed to arise”, and encouraged further work on article 21. With respect to workstream 4, reference was made to alternative profit-allocation approaches, including a suggestion to extend the fractional apportionment method of article 12B to all services. Regarding workstream 6, one member cautioned against scope creep.12.Several members raised practical questions about implementation, including how members expected to work on workstreams 4 and 5 would be involved during the earlier phases, whether the programme could be delivered within time and resource constraints and whether additional drafting support, including from consultants, might be needed. The need for a clear risk mitigation strategy was also emphasized.13.Ms. Kiarie clarified that workstreams 1 to 3 had been sequenced first because they addressed immediate priorities for developing countries and did not depend on the outputs of other subcommittees. She further noted that, while formal consideration of workstreams 4 and 5 was expected to follow the October 2026 outputs of the relevant subcommittees, preliminary work on those issues could begin earlier. Mr. Guici added that this sequencing did not diminish the importance of workstreams 4 and 5 and stressed the need for a sound analytical basis before any possible amendments in that area. The Co-Coordinators indicated that the comments made would be taken into account in the Subcommittee’s further work. The Committee subsequently approved the workplan.B.Update of the United Nations Manual for the Negotiation of Bilateral Tax Treaties between Developed and Developing Countries14.The Co-Coordinator of the Subcommittee on the Update of the United Nations Manual for the Negotiation of Bilateral Tax Treaties between Developed and Developing Countries, Gian Sandri, speaking also on behalf of his Co-Coordinator, Carlos Protto, introduced conference room paper E/C.18/2026/CRP.2 containing the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan. He described the Manual as a practical tool for treaty negotiators, particularly those with less experience, intended to provide concise guidance on negotiation techniques and article-by-article issues under the United Nations Model Tax Convention. The proposed work would proceed through two workstreams and a two-phase approach, with initial priority given to aligning the Manual with the 2025 United Nations Model Tax Convention and a second phase addressing practical negotiation challenges and possible further improvements. Mr. Sandri outlined the proposed timetable for the work within the current membership and invited the Committee to review and approve the proposed workplan.15.During the discussion, questions were raised regarding whether the two-phase approach might delay work under workstream 2. Several members supported the initial prioritization of workstream 1, while emphasizing that workstream 2 should also be clearly prioritized, finalized and completed within the current mandate. In that connection, particular priority was proposed for guidance on the renegotiation of existing treaties, as well as on issues such as most-favoured-nation clauses and hybrid negotiations. Mr. Sandri clarified that the two-phase approach related primarily to drafting sequencing and did not mean that workstream 2 would be deferred. He confirmed that preparatory work on workstream 2 would begin while drafting under workstream 1 was under way and that workstream 2 would be completed within the current membership, with flexibility relating only to the precise scope and extent of the guidance.16.Comments also focused on the scope of the proposed workstreams. Several members highlighted the value of developing more systematic guidance on joint strategies and the combined negotiation of interlinked provisions, noting that such guidance would be useful both for negotiations and training purposes. Attention was also drawn to the importance of practical guidance tailored to the challenges faced by developing countries in treaty negotiations and to the need for the Manual to be accessible. Mr. Sandri confirmed that guidance on joint strategies and the combined negotiation of interlinked provisions would form an important part of workstream 2.17.Several members and observers drew attention to most-favoured-nation clauses, stressing the need for practical drafting examples. They highlighted both the possible usefulness of such clauses in helping negotiating parties reach agreement and the implementation difficulties those clauses could create. Others emphasized that the Manual should also address the risks and possible detrimental effects of most-favoured-nation clauses for developing countries, including in relation to revenue mobilization, and should draw on recent experience to provide guidance in situations where their inclusion could not be avoided. Mr. Sandri indicated that the Manual would address both drafting issues and the possible advantages and disadvantages of most-favoured-nation clauses, including situations in which they might operate to the detriment of developing countries. He welcomed further practical examples and feedback to help determine how such experience could best be reflected in the Manual.18.Members sought further clarification on how the Subcommittee’s work would be coordinated with that of other relevant subcommittees and on how future amendments to the United Nations Model Tax Convention might be reflected in the Manual. Mr. Sandri clarified that updates to the Manual could follow only after substantive changes to the Model Convention had been finalized, meaning that some delay was inevitable. In exceptional cases, however, particularly rapid progress on specific amendments might allow them to be reflected in the Manual within the current membership. He added that the Subcommittee would continue to coordinate closely with the other subcommittees.19.One member proposed that the work should consider impact assessment, including an analysis of the effect of new measures and what would be required of countries to assess that effect. An observer emphasized the need to maintain coherence across the Committee’s outputs in light of developments in the digitalized economy and their implications for the extractive industries and automation. In response, Mr. Sandri noted that impact analysis was important in treaty preparation and renegotiation, while acknowledging that the Manual could not be a substitute for case-specific assessments of individual treaties.20.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on the Update of the United Nations Manual for the Negotiation of Bilateral Tax Treaties between Developed and Developing Countries.C.Transfer pricing21.The Co-Coordinator of the Subcommittee on Transfer Pricing, Trude Steinnes Sønvisen, speaking also on behalf of her Co-Coordinators, Mathew Gbonjubola and Wanda Montero, presented the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan, as contained in conference room paper E/C.18/2026/CRP.3. She recalled that the Committee had decided at its thirty-first session to establish the Subcommittee with a mandate to propose updates to the 2021 United Nations Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries, develop sector-specific guidance, develop guidance on unilateral advance pricing agreements and liaise with the Subcommittee on the Update of the United Nations Model Tax Convention and the Subcommittee on Taxation of the Digitalized and Globalized Economy on possible work relating to profit attribution to permanent establishments.22.Ms. Sønvisen outlined the four proposed areas of work. First, on updating the Manual, the Subcommittee proposed to revise chapter 5 on intragroup services, with a focus on the benefit test; update chapter 6 on intangibles to, for example, address bundled transactions; and update chapter 9 on financial transactions to cover cash pooling transactions and the classification of debt and equity. The Subcommittee also proposed to expand guidance on simplification measures, including safe harbours, and on country-risk adjustments. Second, for sector-specific guidance, the Subcommittee proposed to focus on the information and communications technology (ICT) sector, given its particular relevance to developing countries, with the exact scope of the guidance to be determined by the Subcommittee. Third, the Subcommittee proposed to develop guidance on unilateral advance pricing agreements, building on guidance on bilateral advance pricing agreements produced by the previous membership. Drafting for these products would be undertaken on an iterative basis, with the Subcommittee presenting guidance products for discussion and approval as they became ready. Fourth, on profit attribution to permanent establishments, the Subcommittee was working on an initial report on possible work in that area to be presented at the thirty-third session of the Committee.23.Members and observers welcomed the proposed workplan and expressed support for its approval. A member highlighted the importance of the work on simplification measures, including safe harbours, for reducing compliance burdens and improving administrative efficiency in developing countries.24.Several members welcomed the proposed focus on the ICT sector, given the sector’s rapid pace of innovation and reliance on intangible assets. Members also requested that the Subcommittee produce guidance for the tourism sector, given its significance as a source of foreign direct investment for many developing countries and its susceptibility to tax avoidance.25.Several members stressed the value of guidance on unilateral advance pricing agreements for developing countries, noting their relatively smaller treaty networks, and emphasized that such guidance could serve as a practical starting point for developing countries to gain experience before progressing to bilateral and multilateral processes.26.A member queried how the work on profit attribution to permanent establishments would interact with the other parts of the Subcommittee’s mandate, given that profit attribution could potentially engage principles that went beyond the arm’s length principle. An observer requested further clarification on the scope of that work.27.The Co-Coordinators acknowledged the suggestion to produce guidance for the tourism sector and noted that the choice of the ICT sector had reflected both research on profit-shifting risks in that sector and expertise available within the Subcommittee. Work on further sectors could be considered at a later point subject to resource availability. On profit attribution to permanent establishments, the Co-Coordinators indicated that the work would be based on the current provisions of the United Nations Model Tax Convention and focus on identifying practical challenges facing developing countries, with a view to producing an initial report on possible work and informing subsequent deliberations across the relevant subcommittees.28.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Transfer Pricing and took note of the organization of work and the timeline for deliverables.D.Taxation issues related to the digitalized and globalized economy29.The Co-Coordinator of the Subcommittee on Taxation of the Digitalized and Globalized Economy, Angie Clocheret, speaking also on behalf of her CoCoordinators, Claudia Pimentel da Silva and Mathew Gbonjubola, presented the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan as contained in conference room paper E/C.18/2026/CRP.4.30.Ms. Clocheret noted that the Subcommittee had been established at the thirty-first session of the Committee and that its mandate required the preparation of two concrete and connected outputs. The first was a focused evaluation report assessing the treatment of services permanent establishments in the 2025 United Nations Model Tax Convention and whether services related to emerging technologies were adequately addressed in the Model Convention, including under articles 12AA and 12B. The second was a practical implementation guide designed to assist countries in applying the services-related provisions of the Model Convention effectively, with particular regard to countries with varying levels of administrative capacity. The evaluation report was scheduled for presentation at the thirty-third session of the Committee, and the implementation guide was to be completed no later than the thirty-sixth session.31.Ms. Clocheret explained that, given the breadth of the mandate, the Subcommittee proposed to work in two sequential phases. Phase 1 would commence immediately and focus on the evaluation report, to be completed through two subgroups working in parallel. Phase 2 would begin following the thirty-third session and would entail work on the implementation guide.32.Members and observers welcomed the proposed workplan. Several members commended the phased approach as a sound and pragmatic structure and, along with a country observer, stressed the need for close and sustained coordination with relevant subcommittees.33.Several members intervened on the scope of the evaluation report on the treatment of services permanent establishments. Some argued that situations without physical presence should be considered broadly, without a narrow focus on services. Members also encouraged the Subcommittee to look beyond article 5 (3) (b) and consider article 5 (3) (a) in its analysis. An observer stressed the need for coordination rules, possibly in the form of a hierarchy, among articles 5 (3) (b), 12AA and 12B.34.One member suggested that the evaluation report examine whether the definition of automated digital services in article 12B needed to be updated in light of developments in artificial intelligence. Another member suggested introducing the option of net taxation in article 12AA.35.A member drew attention to the need to distinguish between different categories of nexus situations: those involving a physical permanent establishment, those involving payment without physical presence and those involving value creation without either. The member highlighted the need for early and ongoing coordination with the Subcommittee on Transfer Pricing on profit attribution arising from any recommended new nexus rules.36.On the topic of emerging technologies, the taxation of the metaverse was identified as a potential field for work. Cryptoassets and related activities were also highlighted as warranting analysis. One country observer noted that the question of whether modern technology constituted a service, a royalty or business profit under article 7 should be analysed by the Subcommittee. One member stressed the need to future-proof the Committee’s work in this area, while an observer emphasized the importance of classifying modern business models according to the degree of human involvement, level of automation and user interaction.37.One member noted the importance of avoiding duplication with discussions taking place in other international forums, while recognizing that the Committee had a distinct mandate and, as underlined by an observer, the work could be of a complementary nature, especially in relation to the ongoing negotiations towards a United Nations framework convention on international tax cooperation. Another observer noted that the Subcommittee should consider recently released guidance from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development on home and services permanent establishments.38.Business representatives emphasized the importance of consulting and engaging with the private sector and the need for economic analysis, and they called for the exemption of services permanent establishments arising from business activities of an exploratory nature.39.The Co-Coordinators thanked members and observers for their input and clarified that article 5 (3) (b) had been cited in the mandate as an illustrative starting point, leaving the Subcommittee free to examine related provisions, including article 5 (3) (a), where interactions arose. They noted that the mandate of the Subcommittee on the Update of the United Nations Model Tax Convention was broader and tasked with analysing nexus more broadly. The Co-Coordinators stressed that comments on interlinkages and the need for coordination would be taken into account. They also invited business representatives to contribute to the work of the Subcommittee, especially through input on emerging business models.40.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Taxation of the Digitalized and Globalized Economy and took note of the organization of work, including the two parallel subgroups established for work on the evaluation report, and the timeline for deliverables.E.Tax administration and artificial intelligence41.The Co-Coordinators of the Subcommittee on Tax Administration and Artificial Intelligence, Jeneba Bangura and Alexander Smirnov, presented the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan, as set out in conference room paper E/C.18/2026/CRP.5. They recalled that the Subcommittee had been established at the thirty-first session of the Committee and was mandated to prepare a draft practical guide to implementing artificial intelligence for tax administrations, primarily designed to assist tax administrations in developing countries. The presentation emphasized that the proposed guide would be practical, modular and adaptable to different levels of digital maturity, with a focus on helping tax administrations first with foundational issues before potentially progressing to more advanced applications in a manner consistent with their capacities and needs.42.Ms. Bangura explained that the guide would be structured around five chapters: (a) an introduction, describing the purpose, scope and context of the publication; (b) key enablers for responsible artificial intelligence adoption; (c) potential artificial intelligence use cases by tax administrations; (d) potential safeguards, including legal and ethical considerations; and (e) conclusions. She noted that the work would prioritize practical examples and case studies, and it would address issues such as fraud detection, risk assessment and mitigation, taxpayer services, governance frameworks and safeguards, including guidance on data, potential gender biases, integrity and confidentiality, in alignment with the Subcommittee’s mandate. She also highlighted linkages with other subcommittees, including those on indirect taxes, wealth taxation and tax and gender, and outlined a timeline for the presentation of chapters at the thirty-third session, a first comprehensive draft at the thirty-fourth session and a second draft for review and approval at the thirty-fifth session.43.Members and observers expressed broad support for the proposed workplan and welcomed the initiative as timely and highly relevant for developing countries. Several members underscored the value of the modular approach, while encouraging the Subcommittee to ensure that the guidance remained practical and directly usable, including through implementation pathways, step-by-step guidance and readiness assessments reflecting differing levels of administrative and technological maturity, and they suggested possible case studies based on their countries’ experiences. The importance of distinguishing between foundational and advanced uses of artificial intelligence, as well as between lower-risk and higher-risk applications, was also highlighted. One member referred to the environmental costs associated with artificial intelligence and potential linkages with the work of the Subcommittee on Environmental Taxation.44.Members and observers also discussed the constraints faced by developing countries, including infrastructure gaps, uneven connectivity, limited data quality, shortages of skilled personnel and the broader digital and skills divides. They highlighted the importance of embedding and strengthening capacity-building for tax administration officials to help guide this transformational process and repeatedly stressed the importance of human oversight and institutional readiness, including the need to address privacy concerns and the legal and institutional frameworks for the effective and responsible use of artificial intelligence.45.Members and observers further noted the importance of high-quality data, preserving confidentiality and ensuring transparency and accountability, especially in the context of preserving taxpayer rights and ensuring that artificial intelligence enhanced rather than replaced human decision-making. They also stressed the importance of assessing legal exposure, litigation risks, digital sovereignty, outsourcing choices and the cost implications of artificial intelligence adoption and maintenance. The potential for the guidance to enhance coordination across public agencies where different authorities used artificial intelligence tools across related areas was also highlighted.46.Members and observers pointed to additional use cases and emerging issues, including the potential for artificial intelligence to assist with broadening the tax base by identifying informal economic activity and supporting targeted outreach, as well as its usefulness for transfer pricing compliance, fraud detection and risk assessment. It was also suggested that the guide should consider the potential asymmetry between sophisticated taxpayers using artificial intelligence tools and tax administrations with more limited capabilities, and that the guide remain sufficiently flexible to adapt to rapid technological changes.47.The Co-Coordinators indicated that the issues raised – including privacy, data protection, human capacity, infrastructure, costs, the informal sector and the distinction between artificial intelligence-assisted analysis and human decision-making – would be reflected in the Subcommittee’s work.48.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Tax Administration and Artificial Intelligence.F.Taxation of the extractive industries49.The Coordinator of the Subcommittee on Extractive Industries Taxation, Darlingston Talery, presented the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan (E/C.18/2026/ CRP.6), which was structured around two main workstreams: (a) the valuation and value addition of critical minerals; and (b) the monitoring of developments in energy transition taxation. He noted that the increasing global demand for critical minerals, coupled with price volatility and information asymmetries, posed significant challenges for tax policy and administration, particularly in developing countries.50.Under the first workstream, the Subcommittee proposed a comprehensive framework organized into four components. The first addressed the broader context, including market dynamics, regional implications and structural challenges faced by resource-rich developing countries. Under the second, key characteristics of the taxation of the extractive industries would be examined, including the role of fiscal regimes, contractual arrangements, tax incentives and stabilization clauses, as well as persistent capacity constraints. The third was focused on administrative issues, highlighting the need for strengthened compliance mechanisms, inter-agency coordination and the use of tools such as country-by-country reporting to enhance risk assessment. The fourth addressed value addition, including downstream processing, customs valuation challenges and risks associated with cross-border transactions and transfer pricing.51.The second workstream comprised a monitoring exercise to track fiscal and taxation developments related to the energy transition, including carbon pricing instruments, tax incentives for clean energy investments, carbon capture and storage measures, and tax expenditures linked to climate commitments. Mr. Talery emphasized the importance of keeping abreast of evolving international practices to ensure that developing countries were equipped to respond effectively to emerging tax policy challenges.52.Members and observers broadly welcomed the proposed workplan and its alignment with the Subcommittee’s mandate. Several emphasized the importance of strengthening coordination with other subcommittees, particularly the Subcommittee on Transfer Pricing. In addition, concerns were raised regarding the interaction between customs valuation and income tax rules, especially where differing valuation objectives could create inconsistencies.53.Capacity constraints in developing countries were highlighted as a central challenge. Members and observers underscored the need for the Subcommittee’s outputs to include practical, accessible guidance and, where appropriate, minimum standards or benchmarks to support tax administrations. The issue of retaining skilled personnel following specialized training was also noted. 54.Transparency and access to information were identified as critical to improving tax outcomes in the extractive sector. Several participants supported greater use of country-by-country reporting and called for enhanced transparency frameworks to address data gaps that hindered effective tax administration. The lack of reliable comparable pricing data for certain critical minerals was highlighted as a key obstacle, and suggestions were made regarding the incorporation of publicly available market information where feasible.55.Members and observers also discussed indirect taxation issues, particularly the challenges associated with value added tax (VAT) in the extractive sector, including persistent refund positions and delays affecting project viability. Emerging technological solutions, such as digital tools for monitoring production and contractual compliance, were noted as potential areas for further exploration.56.Observers also raised legal and contractual issues, including the implications of stabilization clauses and the potential value of developing model contract provisions. Environmental and fiscal issues, including the design of windfall profit taxes and the estimation of long-term decommissioning costs, were also discussed.57.Mr. Talery confirmed that the Subcommittee was committed to integrating key suggestions into its workplan. He also acknowledged that emerging priorities raised by members and observers – including windfall taxation, resource governance and the use of digital technologies such as artificial intelligence and blockchain – were areas to be further developed within the Subcommittee’s work.58.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Extractive Industries Taxation.G.Indirect taxes59.The Co-Coordinators of the Subcommittee on Indirect Taxes, Hajara Batamuliza and Hector Thompson, speaking also on behalf of their fellow Co-Coordinator, Kapembwa Namuyemba-Sikombe, who had been unable to attend the session, introduced their report (E/C.18/2026/CRP.7). They recalled that the Subcommittee had been established at the thirty-first session with a mandate to develop practical guidance on VAT and goods and services tax (GST) policy and administration, paying particular attention to developing countries.60.The Co-Coordinators reported on the initial meetings held to identify priority areas and develop the proposed workplan. They noted the central role of VAT as a key source of revenue for developing countries and highlighted practical challenges, including fraud risks, refund management, small and medium-sized enterprise compliance, digitalization, cross-border transactions and structural design issues.61.Those challenges were grouped into five proposed workstreams: (a) VAT in the digitalized economy; (b) VAT fraud prevention, including refund management and small and medium-sized enterprise compliance; (c) cross-border VAT dispute prevention and resolution; (d) VAT treatment of financial services, particularly financial technology (fintech) and cryptoasset transactions; and (e) VAT regressivity and the consideration of compensation or redistribution mechanisms. The CoCoordinators also noted the linkages with other Committee workstreams and outlined a phased workplan, indicating that further refinement would be required for the workstream on VAT regressivity.62.Members expressed broad support for the proposed workplan and welcomed its practical orientation. Several members highlighted the importance of VAT in the digitalized economy, including platform-based business models and cross-border supplies, as well as the role of digital tools, such as e-invoicing and real-time data, in strengthening compliance and addressing fraud risks. 63.Members also highlighted practical implementation challenges in the digital context, including the registration of non-resident suppliers, the role of intermediaries and deemed supplier rules, and the use of proxies, such as customer location data, to determine taxing rights. The need to develop approaches suited to different levels of administrative capacity was noted.64.Differing views were expressed regarding the scope of the workplan. One member suggested limiting it to four workstreams to ensure feasibility and timely delivery. Several members, however, underscored the importance of addressing VAT regressivity, noting its relevance for developing countries and potential impact on vulnerable groups, including low-income households, as well as gender-related considerations. It was suggested that the workstream be retained, subject to further refinement.65.Members also raised cross-cutting issues, including the interaction between VAT and other tax instruments, such as digital services taxes. They stressed the importance of maintaining clarity on the nature of VAT as an indirect tax, particularly in relation to treaty frameworks.66.Observers stressed the importance of addressing implementation challenges faced by developing countries. Suggestions included simplified compliance and registration mechanisms, risk-based refund management frameworks and practical tools for dispute prevention and resolution. Several speakers stressed that guidance should remain practical and accessible, taking into account varying levels of administrative capacity, and noted the importance of early-stage coordination mechanisms.67.Representatives from the private sector and academia highlighted the importance of continued engagement with businesses. They raised concerns regarding the complexity and fragmentation of electronic invoicing systems across jurisdictions, the lack of interoperability across systems and the burden of complying with multiple reporting requirements. Sector-specific challenges, including in aviation and tourism, were also noted, alongside practical difficulties in collecting and managing relevant taxpayer and transaction data.68.Additional interventions highlighted challenges related to digital services and low-value imports, as well as the need for practical guidance tailored to developing country contexts, including on strengthening intermediary-based collection models and leveraging digital platforms as compliance points.69.The Co-Coordinators welcomed the broad support and constructive feedback. They acknowledged the importance of digitalization and real-time data, while noting the challenges of balancing effective VAT collection with input tax credit mechanisms. They noted the differing views on the VAT regressivity workstream and indicated that further consideration would be given to its scope and prioritization. The Co-Coordinators indicated that the comments made would be taken into account in the Subcommittee’s further work and encouraged stakeholders to continue sharing country experiences.70.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Indirect Taxes.H.Dispute avoidance and resolution71.The Coordinator of the Ad Hoc Group on Dispute Avoidance and Resolution, Gian Sandri, introduced his report (E/C.18/2026/CRP.8). He recalled that the Group had been established by the Committee as an ad hoc mechanism and currently functioned as a monitoring body. He outlined the Group’s mandate, which included monitoring developments in dispute avoidance and resolution, monitoring feedback from capacity development activities, identifying linkages with other workstreams and reporting to the Committee.72.Mr. Sandri reported that the Group had held two meetings addressing its composition and identifying key areas for monitoring. At that stage, no revisions to the United Nations Handbook on the Avoidance and Resolution of Tax Disputes (published in 2021) were considered necessary. The Group would focus on monitoring developments in international forums, including: (a) developments under workstream III of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee on the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, particularly those relating to the draft protocol on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes; (b) developments under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)/Group of 20 (G20) inclusive framework, including aspects of pillar 2 relating to dispute resolution; and (c) feedback from capacity development activities. He noted that the drafting phase under workstream III had begun, in which issues such as scope, optionality and dispute resolution in the absence of tax treaties were being addressed. Upcoming capacity development activities, including workshops on the mutual agreement procedure and advance pricing agreements, were also noted.73.One member emphasized the relevance of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, for dispute prevention, noting their potential use in risk identification, fraud detection and early warning systems.74.Observers emphasized the importance of dispute prevention, particularly for developing countries, and highlighted capacity constraints associated with existing mechanisms, such as the mutual agreement procedure. Suggestions were made regarding, inter alia, clearer treaty drafting, the development of practical guidance and the need to ensure that arbitration mechanisms remained voluntary and balanced.75.The Coordinator acknowledged the relevance of emerging technologies and noted their dual role in dispute prevention and risk detection. He emphasized the importance of capacity development, institutional stability and trust-building between competent authorities and noted that arbitration should remain balanced and voluntary.76.The Committee took note of the report of the Ad Hoc Group and approved the workplan contained therein.I.Environmental taxation77.The Co-Coordinators of the Subcommittee on Environmental Taxation, Giedrė Lideikytė Huber and Susanne Åkerfeldt, presented the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan (E/C.18/2026/CRP.9). Recalling the Subcommittee’s mandate to develop practical guidance on policy and administrative issues in the design and implementation of environmental taxes, with a primary focus on carbon taxation, they proposed a comprehensive workplan comprising six thematic workstreams. 78.The first workstream was focused on the transition from fuel excise taxes to carbon-based taxes. Under that workstream, practical approaches to redesigning existing excise systems to reflect carbon content while maintaining revenue stability and administrative simplicity would be examined. The second workstream addressed taxation of emissions in aviation, including both domestic and international dimensions, and the sector’s current tax treatment, its climate impact and the need for international coordination would be considered.79.Under the third workstream, environmental taxation of land-based resources, including forestry, land use and biodiversity, would be examined with a view to developing fiscal measures that discourage environmentally harmful practices and promote sustainable resource management. The fourth workstream was focused on the equity impacts of environmental taxes; distributional effects would be assessed and mechanisms such as revenue recycling would be explored to mitigate adverse impacts on vulnerable groups and ensure public acceptability. The fifth workstream would provide an analytical overview of legal frameworks and recent international developments, including emerging climate-related legal obligations. Under the sixth workstream, the environmental taxation of digital infrastructure, including energy-intensive technologies such as data centres and artificial intelligence systems, would be explored as a forward-looking area of policy development.80.The Co-Coordinators also outlined an implementation timeline, including initial reporting in 2026, progressive development of draft guidance in 2027 and 2028 and finalization of outputs by 2029. They emphasized coordination with other subcommittees, including those on Extractive Industries Taxation, Indirect Taxes and the Update of the United Nations Model Tax Convention, as well as engagement with a broad range of stakeholders.81.Members and observers broadly welcomed the workplan, noting its ambition, relevance and potential contribution to international guidance on environmental taxation. 82.Members and observers highlighted a number of substantive issues for further consideration. These included the need to ensure that unintended double taxation was avoided and fiscal stability was preserved during the transition from fuel excise taxes to carbon-based taxes. With respect to aviation, the importance of taking into account existing international frameworks and of ensuring coordinated approaches to avoid market distortions was emphasized, alongside the need to assess potential impacts on connectivity, tourism-dependent economies and trade.83.The importance of addressing equity considerations was strongly underscored. Members and observers called for greater attention to the distributional impacts of environmental taxes, including gender dimensions and household-level effects, and highlighted the role of targeted revenue recycling mechanisms in maintaining public support for reforms. Several members and observers also emphasized the need to strike a balance between environmental objectives and broader economic considerations, particularly in developing countries.84.Methodological considerations were also discussed, including the need to strengthen the evidence underpinning policy recommendations, ensure administrative feasibility and compile relevant economic and regulatory impact analyses. The importance of stakeholder engagement, including with the private sector, was highlighted, and particular emphasis was placed on the need to ensure that policy frameworks were predictable and implementable.85.The Co-Coordinators indicated that the comments shared would be taken into account in a pragmatic way, with a balance being struck between emerging issues and existing priorities and resource constraints. Ms. Lideikytė Huber highlighted the strong interlinkage between the environmental impact of fast fashion and aviation emissions and underscored the technical complexity of taxing aviation, including underappreciated non-CO2 effects, while noting the need to consider the frameworks of the International Civil Aviation Organization during the Subcommittee’s work. Ms. Åkerfeldt emphasized the importance of maintaining a focused and feasible workplan while remaining open to additional areas where appropriate.86.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Environmental Taxation.J.Wealth taxation87.The Coordinator of the Subcommittee on Wealth Taxation, Jorge Alberto Ferreras Gutiérrez, presented the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan (E/C.18/2026/ CRP.10). He recalled that the Subcommittee had been established at the thirty-first session with a mandate to develop further draft guidance on policy and administrative issues in the design and implementation of wealth taxation, including the taxation of high-net-worth individuals, building on the United Nations Handbook on Wealth and Solidarity Taxes, paying particular attention to the priorities and challenges of developing countries and giving due consideration to issues related to tax transparency.88.Mr. Ferreras Gutiérrez outlined the Subcommittee’s proposal to produce a handbook on the taxation of high-net-worth individuals. A holistic approach would be adopted for the handbook, which would cover: the definition of high-net-worth individual in a manner flexible enough to reflect different wealth concentration profiles across countries; strategies commonly used by such individuals to engage in tax avoidance and evasion; the policy instruments and domestic legislative measures available to address those strategies, including anti-avoidance rules and exit taxes; international and multilateral measures under discussion; the development of specialized administrative units within tax administrations; and the role of tax transparency and exchange of information. Those issues would be illustrated with case studies and practical examples, where possible.89.The Subcommittee proposed to present an outline of the handbook at the thirty-third session, with subsequent drafts presented for discussion and approval at later sessions, with a view to completing the handbook at the thirty-seventh session, at the latest. Mr. Ferreras Gutiérrez also noted that the Subcommittee, in close liaison with the Subcommittee on the Update of the United Nations Model Tax Convention, was open to contributing to an examination of whether changes to article 22 of the Model Convention might be warranted in light of the completion of the United Nations sample net wealth tax law.90.Members and observers welcomed the proposed workplan, recognizing the growing political importance of inequality and the importance of the Committee addressing that issue.91.Members underscored the challenges faced by tax administrations in exchanging information on mobile assets, including financial instruments and artwork; the risks associated with capital and individual mobility; and the need for practical guidance on identifying ultimate beneficial ownership while preserving taxpayer confidentiality. They also noted that, while multilateral coordination was the ideal solution, domestic measures were important. In that regard, particular attention was paid to the appropriate design of capital income taxes and exit taxes, changes to the definition of and criteria for tax residence, measures aimed at closing existing loopholes in domestic tax codes, the strengthening of anti-evasion norms, the use of emerging technologies to detect tax fraud and the organizational design of tax administrations.92.One member also drew attention to the potential relevance of reviewing additional articles of the Model Convention beyond article 22 (Capital), including article 13 (Capital gains).93.Observers suggested a range of policy instruments that could contribute to the effective taxation of high-net-worth individuals, including a review of citizenship-by-investment programmes, citizenship-based taxation, minimum effective personal income taxes and the strengthening of information exchange and transparency measures, including a global asset register of final beneficiaries. While acknowledging the need to address rising inequality, one observer emphasized the importance of maintaining a balanced approach that did not presume adverse intent on the part of high-net-worth individuals but effectively tackled existing loopholes in domestic tax codes. The interlinkages between the taxation of high-net-worth individuals and environmental taxation were also highlighted.94.Mr. Ferreras Gutiérrez thanked all speakers for their comments and explained how the issues raised would be considered and incorporated into the different sections of the handbook. He also reiterated that appropriate linkages would be maintained with relevant work being conducted in other subcommittees.95.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Wealth Taxation and took note of the timeline for deliverables.K.Tax and gender96.The Co-Coordinator of the Subcommittee on Tax and Gender, Jeneba Bangura, speaking also on behalf of her fellow Co-Coordinator, Kapembwa Namuyemba-Sikombe, introduced the Subcommittee’s proposed workplan (E/C.18/2026/CRP.11) for discussion and approval. Ms. Bangura recalled that the Subcommittee was mandated to develop draft guidance on policy and administrative issues related to the relationship between tax and gender, including in the context of the informal economy.97.Ms. Bangura outlined the Subcommittee’s proposal to prepare five guidance papers on the following topics: (a) an overview of taxation and gender, addressing the conceptual framework, evidence and resources available for developing countries; (b) tax policy and the informal economy from a gender perspective; (c) a toolkit for mainstreaming gender into the work of tax administrations; (d) tax data and gender for adequate policy design; and (e) gender and international taxation.98.Ms. Bangura explained that the first paper would offer an overview of the current landscape and identify priority issues requiring guidance. The second would examine gender-differentiated impacts of tax policies in the context of the informal economy. The third would propose a practical toolkit for integrating gender considerations across tax administration functions, including recruitment, career advancement and organizational processes. The fourth would address the collection and use of gender-disaggregated tax data. The fifth would analyse the relationship between gender and international taxation.99.Ms. Bangura underscored that the papers would be aimed at delivering concise and practical guidance grounded in real-world issues. She highlighted the need for robust coordination, high-quality data and synergies with the Subcommittees on Wealth Taxation, Indirect Taxes and Tax Administration and Artificial Intelligence. She noted that while work on all five papers would proceed concurrently to maintain coherence and avoid an overly broad scope, the conceptual framework set out in the first paper would be prioritized. Smaller groups would work on each paper and hold regular virtual meetings.100.Ms. Bangura presented the proposed timeline, explaining that the Subcommittee expected to present outlines of the papers at the thirty-third session, first drafts at the thirty-fourth session and final versions for review and approval at the thirty-sixth session, and that technical refinements would be undertaken at the thirty-seventh session if necessary. She stressed that appropriate strategies would be put in place to manage risks related to duplication, resource constraints and the ambition of the project, including through adherence to the organization of work, timeline and deliverables set out in the workplan.101.Members and observers welcomed the workplan, its structure and forward-looking approach. They highlighted the value of the proposed gender-mainstreaming toolkit and the analysis of gender and international taxation, while noting that the latter would require careful scoping.102.Members suggested enhancing the workplan and its deliverables by analysing structural and historical inequalities between women and men that affected tax policy; reviewing fiscal measures supporting women’s access to formal employment; taking into consideration differences in norms and attitudes between societies; using practical, context-specific examples; addressing gender bias in existing data sets; and strengthening the focus on gender-responsive taxation in the informal economy. Some members also asked whether the Subcommittee could consider collecting gender-disaggregated data and whether gender-based price differentials in consumer goods would be included in the analysis. The importance of maintaining a focused scope to ensure timely delivery of outputs within the Committee’s mandate was also stressed.103.Observers welcomed the emphasis on practical guidance and evidence-based policymaking. They encouraged striking a balance between revenue objectives and inclusive policies, noting that the latter could help expand the tax base and support growth. They also pointed to the importance of practical guidance on mainstreaming gender into tax administration. One observer encouraged the Subcommittee to consider tax incentives for women-led small and medium-sized enterprises to support formalization and inclusive economic development.104.Ms. Bangura expressed appreciation for the support and constructive suggestions. She confirmed that the Subcommittee would draw extensively from existing data, case studies and research papers, particularly in developing countries. She emphasized that capacity-building was essential across all planned work to ensure the practical uptake of guidance. To that end, she invited members to provide case studies from their respective countries.105.The Committee approved the workplan of the Subcommittee on Tax and Gender.L.Capacity-building106.Caroline Lombardo and Emily Muyaa of the Department of Economic and Social Affairs presented an update on the Department’s capacity development programme on tax and domestic resource mobilization, highlighting its integrated approach that linked international policy development, practical capacity-building and intergovernmental dialogue. Since 2023, the Committee had produced more than 16 guidance products. As part of activities led by the Department, more than 3,294 tax officials had received training through in-person and online workshops, with reported satisfaction rates above 89.5 per cent. Recent activities included workshops on tax treaty negotiation, mutual agreement procedures, transfer pricing and VAT/GST, as well as the dissemination of Committee guidance in multiple languages.107.The Secretariat showed a video illustrating the role of the United Nations Model Convention and summarizing the changes made to the Model Convention by the previous membership, with the goal of broadly disseminating the work of the Committee and showcasing its contribution to sustainable development efforts. 108.The Department also reported growing demand for technical assistance on treaty administration, attribution of profits to permanent establishments, dispute avoidance and resolution, transfer pricing and VAT/GST and outlined workshops planned for 2026.109.The Department expressed appreciation for financial and in-kind contributions from the Government of Norway, the Government of Denmark, the European Union, the Government of India, the Government of Singapore, the regular programme of technical cooperation and other partners in support of the work of the Committee, its subcommittees and related capacity-building activities.110.Members and observers commended the Department on its practical and integrated approach and noted the valuable role it played in translating the Committee’s technical outputs into accessible and operational tools for tax administrations, particularly in developing countries. They stressed the importance of continuing practical, case-based training and widening the dissemination of guidance products to help officials translate international guidance into day-to-day practice. The importance of inclusive participation, including the involvement of the least developed countries and small island developing States, was also highlighted, both in terms of benefitting from capacity development activities and informing the Committee’s work through diverse country perspectives.111.Members and observers also pointed to the value of more systematic longer-term follow-up of activities to assess the extent to which trained officials remained in service and continued to apply the knowledge and skills acquired. Some speakers noted challenges related to staff turnover within tax administrations and emphasized the importance of tracking longer-term impact. In that connection, they highlighted training-of-trainers approaches and stronger internal knowledge-sharing mechanisms as useful tools, alongside measures to support the institutional retention of expertise.112.Several speakers emphasized the importance of mobilizing additional resources to sustain and expand the Department’s capacity development work. They stressed that continued support beyond initial training – including follow-up engagement and technical assistance – was critical to enable countries to implement the Committee’s guidance effectively. Speakers also highlighted the importance of exploring scalable delivery models, including through partnerships with other organizations, to respond to growing demand within resource constraints.M.Other matters for consideration113.No additional matters were raised for consideration.Chapter VProvisional agenda for the thirty-third session114.The Secretariat presented the provisional agenda for the thirty-third session of the Committee, to be held in Geneva from 20 to 23 October 2026, and noted the tentative dates for the thirty-fourth session, to be held in New York from 5 to 8 April 2027. The Committee approved the provisional agenda.Chapter VIArrangements for adopting the report of the Committee on its thirty-second session115.The Secretariat noted that, in accordance with the Committee’s practices and working methods, members would review the draft report within two weeks before its finalization and submission for publication.
